A 2D bar, as a Fortran object

Created with Grok Build

Source code by Jonas Lindemann, from the oop_fortran repository.

simple_frame_2d takes the same type-bound style as the shape classes and uses it for one finite-element object. A bar has two end points, a Young’s modulus, and an area. Its method Ke returns the 4 by 4 stiffness matrix in global coordinates. The program constructs one bar with the defaults, prints that matrix, and constructs a small model of nodes and elements. It does not solve a frame. The commented lines in main are the calls that would have printed the node and element tables.

Each section shows the declaration or the procedure, then what it does. The files are code/simple_frame_2d/mf_datatypes.f90, mf_utils.f90, calfem.f90, and main.f90.

mf_datatypes¶

mf_datatypes.f90
module mf_datatypes

use iso_fortran_env

implicit none

integer, parameter :: dp = real64
integer, parameter :: sp = real32

end module mf_datatypes

dp is real64, a double, from iso_fortran_env. sp is real32. The bar code uses real(dp) for coordinates, EEE, AAA, and KKK. The particle module later in the Qt program is a different file: it also defines an integer kind ik and a double constant pi. The two files share a name and are separate modules, each compiled with its own program.

mf_utils¶

The module keeps the print layout in four variables. Three of them are private.

mf_utils.f90
interface print_matrix
    module procedure print_matrix_d, print_matrix_s, print_matrix_i
end interface

interface print_vector
    module procedure print_vector_d, print_vector_s
end interface

interface rand_mat
    module procedure rand_mat_d, rand_mat_s
end interface

interface rand_vec
    module procedure rand_vec_d, rand_vec_s
end interface

integer, private :: field_width = 10
integer, private :: field_decimals = 4
character :: field_code(1) = 'G'
character :: int_field_code(1) = 'I'

The defaults are width 10, decimals 4, real edit descriptor G, and integer edit descriptor I. Generic interfaces are the overloading. print_matrix can be called with a double matrix, a single matrix, or an integer matrix. The compiler picks print_matrix_d, print_matrix_s, or print_matrix_i from the argument type. print_vector, rand_mat, and rand_vec are the same idea. The bar program only calls the double matrix printer.

set_print_format¶

mf_utils.f90
subroutine set_print_format(width, decimals, code, int_code)

    integer, optional :: width
    integer, optional :: decimals
    character, optional :: code(1)
    character, optional :: int_code(1)

    if (present(width)) then
        field_width = width
    end if

    if (present(decimals)) then
        field_decimals = decimals
    end if

    if (present(code)) then
        field_code = code
    end if

    if (present(int_code)) then
        int_field_code = code
    end if

end subroutine set_print_format

Each argument is optional. A present width replaces field_width. A present decimal count replaces field_decimals. A present one-character code replaces field_code.

The program calls set_print_format(12), so the width becomes 12 and the other three stay at the defaults. The matrix in the output is four numbers per line in a G12.4 field, which is why 7.424621×1067.424621\times 10^67.424621×106 appears as 0.7425E+07.

The integer-code branch assigns int_field_code = code. code is the real edit descriptor, and int_code is the argument that was just tested. The demo never passes int_code, so the printed matrix uses the real descriptor G. A caller who passed an integer code would store code into int_field_code.

print_matrix_d¶

mf_utils.f90
subroutine print_matrix_d(A, name)

    real(dp), intent(in) :: A(:,:)
    character(*), intent(in), optional :: name
    integer :: rows, cols, slen
    integer :: i, j
    character(255) :: fmt
    character(255) :: sfmt

    rows = size(A,1)
    cols = size(A,2)
    slen = len_trim(name)

    if (slen<10) then
        write(sfmt, '(A,I1,A)') '(TL1,A,A',slen,',A,I3,A,I3,A)'
    else if (slen<100) then
        write(sfmt, '(A,I2,A)') '(TL1,A,A',slen,',A,I3,A,I3,A)'
    else
        write(sfmt, '(A,I3,A)') '(TL1,A,A',slen,',A,I3,A,I3,A)'
    end if

    if (cols<10) then
        if (field_width<10) then
            write(fmt, '(A,I1,A,I1,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        else
            write(fmt, '(A,I1,A,I2,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        end if
    else if (cols<100) then
        if (field_width<10) then
            write(fmt, '(A,I2,A,I1,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        else
            write(fmt, '(A,I2,A,I2,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        end if
    else
        if (field_width<10) then
            write(fmt, '(A,I3,A,I1,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        else
            write(fmt, '(A,I3,A,I2,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        end if
    end if

    !write(*,'(TL1,A)') repeat('-', cols*field_width)
    print*,''
    if (present(name)) then
        write(*,sfmt) 'Matrix ',trim(name),' (',rows, ' x ', cols, ') DP'
    else
        write(*,'(TL1,A,I3,A,I3,A)') 'Matrix (',rows, ' x ', cols, ') DP'
    end if
    write(*,'(TL1,A)') repeat('-', cols*field_width)


    do i=1,rows
        write(*,fmt) (A(i,j), j=1,cols)
    end do

    write(*,'(TL1,A)') repeat('-', cols*field_width)

end subroutine print_matrix_d

This is the procedure behind the matrix you see. It reads the row and column counts with size. It builds a title format from the length of the name, and a data format with one G field per column.

For the bar, cols is 4 and set_print_format(12) has set field_width to 12, field_decimals to 4, and field_code to G. The branch taken is the one for fewer than 10 columns and a width of at least 10:

write(fmt, '(A,I1,A,I2,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'

That writes the characters of the format (4G12.4). G12.4 asks for a field 12 characters wide with 4 significant digits. The title line is Matrix Ke ( 4 x 4) DP. The rule of hyphens is cols * field_width characters wide. Each row is one write of that row of the matrix.

The random helpers¶

mf_utils.f90
subroutine rand_mat_d(A, randMin, randMax)

    real(dp), intent(inout) :: A(:,:)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(A)

    !    min ---- max

    A = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * A

end subroutine rand_mat_d

random_number fills A with values UUU in [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1). The next line scales that into the requested range:

A=amin⁡+(amax⁡−amin⁡) UA = a_{\min} + (a_{\max} - a_{\min})\, UA=amin​+(amax​−amin​)U
(1)

randMin + (randMax-randMin) * A is that formula. The comment min ---- max is the same interval.

mf_utils.f90
subroutine rand_mat_s(A, randMin, randMax)

    real(sp), intent(inout) :: A(:,:)
    real(sp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(A)

    !    min ---- max

    A = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * A

end subroutine rand_mat_s
mf_utils.f90
subroutine rand_vec_d(a, randMin, randMax)

    real(dp), intent(inout) :: a(:)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(a)

    !    min ---- max

    a = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * a

end subroutine rand_vec_d
mf_utils.f90
subroutine rand_vec_s(a, randMin, randMax)

    real(sp), intent(inout) :: a(:)
    real(sp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(a)

    !    min ---- max

    a = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * a

end subroutine rand_vec_s

rand_mat_s, rand_vec_d, and rand_vec_s implement the same scaling for a single-precision matrix and for a double or single vector. The bar program does not call any of them.

mf_utils.f90
subroutine init_rand()
    integer :: values(1:8), k
    integer, dimension(:), allocatable :: seed
    real(real64) :: r
    call date_and_time(values=values)
    call random_seed(size=k)
    allocate(seed(1:k))
    seed(:) = values(8)
    call random_seed(put=seed)
end subroutine

init_rand calls random_seed with no argument on the size inquiry, then stores values(8) into every seed element. values(8) from date_and_time is the millisecond field. The local r is declared and never used. The bar program does not call init_rand.

NodeSet¶

calfem.f90
interface NodeSet
    module procedure node_set_constructor
end interface NodeSet

type NodeSet
    real(dp), allocatable :: m_positions(:,:)
    integer, allocatable :: m_dofs(:,:)
contains
    procedure :: init => node_set_init
    procedure :: print => node_set_print
    procedure :: resize => node_set_resize
    final :: node_set_destructor
end type

A node set is the mesh’s node table: m_positions(n_nodes, 2) and m_dofs(n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node). Nothing is private. A caller can write the arrays directly. The bindings are init, print, resize, and a finalizer.

interface NodeSet makes NodeSet(n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node) call node_set_constructor.

node_set_init¶

calfem.f90
subroutine node_set_init(this, n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node)

    class(NodeSet) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: n_nodes
    integer, intent(in) :: n_dofs_per_node

    allocate(this % m_positions(n_nodes, 2))
    allocate(this % m_dofs(n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node))

    this % m_positions = 0.0_dp
    this % m_dofs = -1

end subroutine

Allocates the two arrays, sets every coordinate to 0, and sets every degree of freedom to -1. -1 means the degree of freedom has not been numbered yet. The constructor is the only caller in this program, with 4 nodes and 2 degrees of freedom per node.

node_set_print¶

calfem.f90
subroutine node_set_print(this)

    class(NodeSet) :: this

    call print_matrix(this % m_positions, 'Positions')
    call print_matrix_i(this % m_dofs, 'Dofs')

end subroutine

Calls print_matrix on the coordinates and print_matrix_i on the degree-of-freedom table. main builds a node set and leaves the print commented out.

node_set_resize¶

calfem.f90
subroutine node_set_resize(this, n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node)

    class(NodeSet) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: n_nodes
    integer, intent(in) :: n_dofs_per_node

    real(dp), allocatable :: positions(:,:)
    integer, allocatable :: dofs(:,:)

    allocate(positions(size(this % m_positions, 1), size(this % m_positions, 2)))
    allocate(dofs(size(this % m_dofs, 1), size(this % m_dofs, 2)))

    positions = this % m_positions
    dofs = this % m_dofs

    deallocate(this % m_positions, this % m_dofs)

    allocate(this % m_positions(n_nodes, 2))
    allocate(this % m_dofs(n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node))

    this % m_positions = 0.0_dp
    this % m_dofs = -1

    if (size(this % m_positions, 1) >= size(positions, 1)) then
        this % m_positions(1:size(positions, 1), :) = positions
    else
        this % m_positions(:,:) = positions(1:size(this % m_positions), :)
    end if

    deallocate(positions, dofs)

end subroutine

Allocates copies of the old arrays, copies both, drops the old allocation, allocates the new shape, fills it with zeros and -1, and copies old coordinates back when the new row count is at least the old row count. The saved degree-of-freedom copy is never written back. deallocate(positions, dofs) drops it with the temporary coordinate copy. A resize would keep coordinates and reset every dof to -1. The program does not call resize.

node_set_destructor¶

calfem.f90
subroutine node_set_destructor(this)

    type(NodeSet) :: this

    print*, 'node_set_destructor'

    deallocate(this % m_positions, this % m_dofs)

end subroutine

Prints node_set_destructor and deallocates both arrays. The dummy is type(NodeSet), the finalizer form. This is the finalizer the run does print. When it runs is under BarModel below.

node_set_constructor¶

calfem.f90
function node_set_constructor(n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node) result(node_set)

    type(NodeSet) :: node_set
    integer, intent(in) :: n_nodes
    integer, intent(in) :: n_dofs_per_node

    print*, 'node_set_constructor'

    call node_set_init(node_set, n_nodes, n_dofs_per_node)

end function

Prints node_set_constructor and calls node_set_init. The result is a function temporary. The finalizer runs as soon as that temporary has been copied into the allocatable component that stores it. That is why the output prints the constructor and the destructor on consecutive lines, while the model still holds a live node set.

ElementSet¶

calfem.f90
interface ElementSet
    module procedure element_set_constructor
end interface ElementSet

type ElementSet
    integer, allocatable :: m_topo(:,:)
contains
    procedure :: init => element_set_init
    procedure :: print => element_set_print
    procedure :: resize => element_set_resize
end type

An element set stores topology in m_topo(n_elements, n_dofs_per_element). The integers are element connectivity. The bindings are init, print, and resize. There is a subroutine element_set_destructor, and it is not registered with final, so the language does not call it. The run does not print element_set_destructor.

element_set_init¶

calfem.f90
subroutine element_set_init(this, n_topo, n_dofs_per_element)

    class(ElementSet) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: n_topo
    integer, intent(in), optional :: n_dofs_per_element

    if (present(n_dofs_per_element)) then
        allocate(this % m_topo(n_topo, n_dofs_per_element))
    else
        allocate(this % m_topo(n_topo, 6))
    end if

    this % m_topo = -1

end subroutine

If the degree-of-freedom count is present, the topology has that many columns. If it is absent, the column count is 6. Every entry starts at -1.

element_set_print¶

calfem.f90
subroutine element_set_print(this)

    class(ElementSet) :: this

    call print_matrix(this % m_topo, 'Topo')

end subroutine

Prints the topology through the generic print_matrix, which selects print_matrix_i because m_topo is integer. main does not call it.

element_set_resize¶

calfem.f90
subroutine element_set_resize(this, n_topo, n_dofs_per_element)

    class(ElementSet) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: n_topo
    integer, intent(in), optional :: n_dofs_per_element

    integer, allocatable :: topo(:,:)
    integer :: actual_n_dofs_per_element


    if (present(n_dofs_per_element)) then
        actual_n_dofs_per_element = n_dofs_per_element
    else
        actual_n_dofs_per_element = 6
    end if


    allocate(topo(size(this % m_topo, 1), size(this % m_topo, 2)))

    topo = this % m_topo

    deallocate(this % m_topo)

    allocate(this % m_topo(n_topo, actual_n_dofs_per_element))

    this % m_topo = -1

    if (size(this % m_topo, 1) >= size(topo, 1)) then
        this % m_topo(1:size(topo, 1), 1:size(topo,2)) = topo
    else
        this % m_topo(:,1:size(topo,2)) = topo(1:size(this % m_topo), 1:size(topo,2))
    end if

    deallocate(topo)

end subroutine

Saves the old topology, reallocates, fills with -1, and copies the overlapping corner back. This copy does get written back. The program does not call resize.

element_set_destructor¶

calfem.f90
subroutine element_set_destructor(this)

    type(ElementSet) :: this

    print*, 'element_set_destructor'

    deallocate(this % m_topo)

end subroutine

Would print element_set_destructor and deallocate m_topo. It is an ordinary subroutine with a type(ElementSet) dummy. No binding points at it.

element_set_constructor¶

calfem.f90
function element_set_constructor(n_topo, n_dofs_per_element) result(element_set)

    type(ElementSet) :: element_set
    integer, intent(in) :: n_topo
    integer, intent(in) :: n_dofs_per_element

    print*, 'node_set_constructor'

    call element_set_init(element_set, n_topo, n_dofs_per_element)

end function

Prints node_set_constructor. The string does not match the subroutine name. The body then calls element_set_init. BarModel does not call this constructor. It calls the bar-element constructor below, which has its own print. This string is absent from the output.

BarElementSet¶

calfem.f90
interface BarElementSet
    module procedure bar_element_set_constructor
end interface BarElementSet

type, extends(ElementSet) :: BarElementSet

contains
    procedure :: init => bar_element_set_init
    procedure :: resize => bar_element_set_resize
end type

BarElementSet extends ElementSet and overrides init and resize. A bar element in 2D has four degrees of freedom, two at each end, so both overrides ignore the passed column count and call the parent with 4.

bar_element_set_init and bar_element_set_resize¶

calfem.f90
subroutine bar_element_set_init(this, n_topo, n_dofs_per_element)

    class(BarElementSet) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: n_topo
    integer, intent(in), optional :: n_dofs_per_element

    call this % elementset % init(n_topo, 4)

end subroutine

subroutine bar_element_set_resize(this, n_topo, n_dofs_per_element)

    class(BarElementSet) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: n_topo
    integer, intent(in), optional :: n_dofs_per_element

    call this % elementset % resize(n_topo, 4)

end subroutine

The parent is named by the parent type. call this % elementset % init(n_topo, 4) is the parent component. It is the same idea as call shape_init(this) in the shape example, written as a component call. call this % init(...) here would recurse into the override. n_dofs_per_element is accepted and then unused. The column count that is stored is the literal 4.

bar_element_set_constructor¶

calfem.f90
function bar_element_set_constructor(n_topo) result(bar_element_set)

    type(BarElementSet) :: bar_element_set
    integer, intent(in) :: n_topo

    print*, 'bar_element_set_constructor'

    call bar_element_set_init(bar_element_set, n_topo, 4)

end function

Prints bar_element_set_constructor and calls bar_element_set_init with the element count and with 4 columns. BarModel calls this once, for 2 elements. The line appears twice in the output for a different reason, described with the program.

BarElement¶

calfem.f90
interface BarElement
    module procedure bar_element_constructor
end interface

type BarElement
    real(dp) :: m_p0(2)
    real(dp) :: m_p1(2)
    real(dp) :: m_A
    real(dp) :: m_E
contains
    procedure :: init => bar_element_init
    procedure :: set_p0 => bar_element_set_p0
    procedure :: set_p1 => bar_element_set_p1
    procedure :: set_ep => bar_element_set_ep
    procedure :: Ke => bar_element_ke
    procedure :: print => bar_element_print
end type

This is the object the matrix comes from. It does not extend ElementSet. A single bar is a separate type from a set of elements. The components are m_p0(2), m_p1(2), m_A, and m_E, all visible. The bindings are init, set_p0, set_p1, set_ep, Ke, and print.

interface BarElement makes BarElement() and BarElement(x0, y0, x1, y1, E, A) call bar_element_constructor. Every argument of that function is optional, so both calls are legal.

bar_element_init¶

calfem.f90
subroutine bar_element_init(this, x0, y0, x1, y1, E, A)

    class(BarElement) :: this
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: x0
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: y0
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: x1
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: y1
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: E
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: A

    this % m_p0 = 0.0_dp
    this % m_p1 = 1.0_dp

    this % m_E = 2.1e9_dp
    this % m_A = 0.1_dp*0.1_dp

    if (present(x0)) this % m_p0(1) = x0
    if (present(x0)) this % m_p0(2) = y0
    if (present(x0)) this % m_p1(1) = x1
    if (present(x0)) this % m_p1(2) = y1
    if (present(x0)) this % m_E = E
    if (present(x0)) this % m_A = A

end subroutine

Sets a default bar, then applies whatever arguments the caller passed.

The defaults are mp0=0m_{p0} = 0mp0​=0 and mp1=1m_{p1} = 1mp1​=1, so the ends are (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) and (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1). The modulus and area are

E=2.1×109,A=0.1×0.1=0.01E = 2.1\times 10^9, \qquad A = 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01E=2.1×109,A=0.1×0.1=0.01
(2)

2.1e9_dp and 0.1_dp*0.1_dp are those two assignments. If the drawing is in metres, EEE is in N/m² and AAA is in m².

The six updates are each guarded by present(x0). y0, x1, y1, E, and A are not the arguments tested. If the caller passes x0, all six are assigned. If the caller passes E and omits x0, the modulus stays at the default. The program calls BarElement() with no arguments, so only the defaults are used and this matrix comes from the defaults.

bar_element_set_p0, bar_element_set_p1, bar_element_set_ep¶

calfem.f90
subroutine bar_element_set_p0(this, x, y)

    class(BarElement) :: this
    real(dp), intent(in) :: x, y

    this % m_p0(1) = x
    this % m_p0(2) = y

end subroutine

subroutine bar_element_set_p1(this, x, y)

    class(BarElement) :: this
    real(dp), intent(in) :: x, y

    this % m_p1(1) = x
    this % m_p1(2) = y

end subroutine

subroutine bar_element_set_ep(this, E, A)

    class(BarElement) :: this
    real(dp), intent(in) :: E, A

    this % m_E = E
    this % m_A = A

end subroutine

set_p0 stores a new first end, set_p1 stores a new second end, and set_ep stores a new modulus and area:

mp0=(x,y),mp1=(x,y),mE=E,mA=Am_{p0} = (x, y), \qquad m_{p1} = (x, y), \qquad m_E = E, \qquad m_A = Amp0​=(x,y),mp1​=(x,y),mE​=E,mA​=A
(3)

main does not call them. They are the way to move the default bar without going back through init.

bar_element_ke¶

calfem.f90
function bar_element_ke(this) result(Ke)

    class(BarElement) :: this
    real(dp) :: Ke(4,4)
    real(dp) :: b(2)
    real(dp) :: L
    real(dp) :: Kle(2,2)
    real(dp) :: c
    real(dp) :: G(2,4)
    real(dp) :: nxx, nyx

    b(1) = this % m_p1(1) - this % m_p0(1)
    b(2) = this % m_p1(2) - this % m_p0(2)

    L = sqrt(dot_product(b,b))

    c = this % m_E * this % m_A / L

    Kle(1,:) = (/ 1.0_dp, -1.0_dp /) * c
    Kle(2,:) = (/-1.0_dp,  1.0_dp /) * c

    nxx = (this % m_p1(1) - this % m_p0(1))/L
    nyx = (this % m_p1(2) - this % m_p0(2))/L

    G(1,:) = (/ nxx, nyx, 0.0_dp, 0.0_dp /)
    G(2,:) = (/ 0.0_dp, 0.0_dp, nxx, nyx /)

    Ke = matmul(transpose(G), matmul(Kle, G))

end function

Returns KeK_eKe​, a 4 by 4 matrix. The four rows and columns are the global degrees of freedom of end 0 in xxx, end 0 in yyy, end 1 in xxx, and end 1 in yyy.

The end-to-end vector and its length are

b=p1−p0,L=b⋅b\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{p}_1 - \mathbf{p}_0, \qquad L = \sqrt{\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{b}}b=p1​−p0​,L=b⋅b​
(4)

b(1) and b(2) are the two components, and L = sqrt(dot_product(b,b)) is the length. The axial stiffness is

c=EALc = \frac{EA}{L}c=LEA​
(5)

which is c = this % m_E * this % m_A / L. In local coordinates, along the bar, the 2 by 2 matrix is

Klocal=c[1−1−11]K_\mathrm{local} = c \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}Klocal​=c[1−1​−11​]
(6)

Kle(1,:) = (/ 1, -1 /) * c and Kle(2,:) = (/ -1, 1 /) * c are those two rows. A positive displacement of end 0 pulls end 1 the other way, which is why the off-diagonals are negative.

G is 2 by 4. Its first row picks out the direction of the bar at end 0, and its second row picks out the same direction at end 1. For a unit vector (nx,ny)(n_x, n_y)(nx​,ny​) along the bar,

nx=p1x−p0xL,ny=p1y−p0yL,G=[nxny0000nxny]n_x = \frac{p_{1x}-p_{0x}}{L}, \qquad n_y = \frac{p_{1y}-p_{0y}}{L}, \qquad G = \begin{bmatrix} n_x & n_y & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & n_x & n_y \end{bmatrix}nx​=Lp1x​−p0x​​,ny​=Lp1y​−p0y​​,G=[nx​0​ny​0​0nx​​0ny​​]
(7)

nxx and nyx are nxn_xnx​ and nyn_yny​. The two assignments to G are the two rows.

The global matrix is

K=GTKlocalGK = G^{T} K_\mathrm{local} GK=GTKlocal​G
(8)

Ke = matmul(transpose(G), matmul(Kle, G)) is that product. matmul(Kle, G) is KlocalGK_\mathrm{local} GKlocal​G, and matmul(transpose(G), ...) multiplies on the left by GTG^TGT.

For the default bar, b=(1,1)\mathbf{b} = (1, 1)b=(1,1), so L=2L = \sqrt{2}L=2​ and (nx,ny)=(1/2, 1/2)(n_x, n_y) = (1/\sqrt{2},\, 1/\sqrt{2})(nx​,ny​)=(1/2​,1/2​). Then

c=2.1×109×0.012=1.484924×107c = \frac{2.1\times 10^9 \times 0.01}{\sqrt{2}} = 1.484924\times 10^7c=2​2.1×109×0.01​=1.484924×107
(9)

Every entry of KKK has magnitude

c2=c(2)2=7.424621×106\frac{c}{2} = \frac{c}{(\sqrt{2})^2} = 7.424621\times 10^62c​=(2​)2c​=7.424621×106
(10)

because each product of direction cosines contributes a factor 1/2×1/2=1/21/\sqrt{2}\times 1/\sqrt{2} = 1/21/2​×1/2​=1/2. The pattern is positive on the two ends’ matching blocks and negative on the coupling blocks. G12.4 prints the magnitude as 0.7425E+07.

bar_element_print¶

calfem.f90
subroutine bar_element_print(this)

    class(BarElement) :: this

    call print_matrix(this % Ke(), 'Ke')

end subroutine

Calls print_matrix on this % Ke(). The matrix is a function result. Printing the bar recomputes KKK.

bar_element_constructor¶

calfem.f90
function bar_element_constructor(x0, y0, x1, y1, E, A) result(bar_element)

    type(BarElement) :: bar_element
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: x0
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: y0
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: x1
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: y1
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: E
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: A

    print*, 'bar_element_set_constructor'

    call bar_element_init(bar_element, x0, y0, x1, y1, E, A)

end function

Prints bar_element_set_constructor. The string names the set constructor. The body then calls bar_element_init with the same optional arguments. BarElement() therefore prints bar_element_set_constructor once, before the matrix. That is the first line of the output, and it is this function. The set routine prints the same words later.

BarModel¶

calfem.f90
interface BarModel
    module procedure bar_model_constructor
end interface

type BarModel
    type(NodeSet), allocatable :: m_node_set
    type(BarElementSet), allocatable :: m_element_set
contains
    procedure :: init => bar_model_init
    procedure :: node_set => bar_model_node_set
    procedure :: element_set => bar_model_element_set
end type

A model owns one allocatable NodeSet and one allocatable BarElementSet. The bindings are init, node_set, and element_set.

bar_model_init¶

calfem.f90
subroutine bar_model_init(this, n_nodes, n_elements)

    class(BarModel) :: this

    integer, intent(in) :: n_nodes
    integer, intent(in) :: n_elements

    this % m_node_set = NodeSet(n_nodes, 2)
    this % m_element_set = BarElementSet(n_elements)

end subroutine

Assigns m_node_set = NodeSet(n_nodes, 2) and m_element_set = BarElementSet(n_elements). The node constructor prints, the temporary is finalized, and the bar-element-set constructor prints. For BarModel(4, 2) that is three lines: node_set_constructor, node_set_destructor, bar_element_set_constructor.

bar_model_node_set and bar_model_element_set¶

calfem.f90
function bar_model_node_set(this) result(node_set)

    class(BarModel) :: this
    type(NodeSet) :: node_set

    node_set = this % m_node_set

end function

function bar_model_element_set(this) result(element_set)

    class(BarModel) :: this
    type(BarElementSet) :: element_set

    element_set = this % m_element_set

end function

Each function returns the component by value, a copy. main leaves both calls commented out. A copy of the node set would be another temporary, and its finalizer would print again.

bar_model_constructor¶

calfem.f90
function bar_model_constructor(n_nodes, n_elements) result(bar_model)

    type(BarModel) :: bar_model
    integer, intent(in) :: n_nodes
    integer, intent(in) :: n_elements

    call bar_model_init(bar_model, n_nodes, n_elements)

end function

Calls bar_model_init and does not print on its own. The lines you see come from the two objects it constructs.

What main prints¶

main.f90
program myfortran

use mf_datatypes
use mf_utils
use calfem

implicit none

type(NodeSet) :: node_set
type(BarElementSet) :: bar_element_set
type(BarElement) :: bar
type(BarModel) :: bar_model

call set_print_format(12)

bar = BarElement()
call bar % print()

bar_model = BarModel(4, 2)
!node_set = bar_model % node_set()
!bar_element_set = bar_model % element_set()

!call bar_element_set % print()

end program myfortran

set_print_format(12) selects the G12.4 layout. bar = BarElement() hits the single-bar constructor, whose print string is bar_element_set_constructor, and bar % print() writes KKK. bar_model = BarModel(4, 2) then builds the tables. node_set and bar_element_set are declared and never used. The commented assignments are what those variables were for.

simple_frame_2d.out
 bar_element_set_constructor

------------------------------------------------

 -0.7425E+07 -0.7425E+07  0.7425E+07  0.7425E+07

------------------------------------------------

The second bar_element_set_constructor is the set constructor, from BarElementSet(2) inside the model. The first one is the single-bar constructor printing those same words.

CMake¶

CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.5)

if (APPLE)
        set(CMAKE_Fortran_COMPILER "/usr/local/bin/gfortran")
endif()

project(simple_frame_2d LANGUAGES Fortran)

set(CMAKE_INCLUDE_CURRENT_DIR ON)

file(GLOB fortran_files *.f90)

add_executable(simple_frame_2d ${fortran_files})

The list is the same shape as the shape program, with the project name simple_frame_2d. cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.5) is the version the list was written for. CMake 3.31 on this machine still configures it. GLOB collects four files: mf_datatypes.f90, mf_utils.f90, calfem.f90, and main.f90. CMake’s Fortran dependency scanner compiles the modules before main.f90. The order in the log is datatypes, utils, calfem, then the program. calfem uses both modules, and main uses all three.
